author: xhigh3
claim: For every prime p>5, admissible infinite sequences are in bijection with pairs (x,y) in (F_p^*\{-1})^2 satisfying x+y+1 != 0; consequently F(p)=(p-2)(p-3).
evidence: Put x=a_1 and y=a_2. Repeated substitution gives a_3=(1+y)/x, a_4=(1+x+y)/(xy), a_5=(1+x)/y, a_6=x, and a_7=y, provided the displayed terms are defined and nonzero. Thus necessity of nonzero terms is exactly y!=-1, x+y+1!=0, x!=-1; conversely these conditions make the five displayed values nonzero and the period-five repetition satisfies every recurrence. There are (p-2)^2 choices with x,y nonzero and unequal to -1. On x+y+1=0, every x in F_p^*\{-1} gives y=-1-x also in F_p^*\{-1}, and conversely, so exactly p-2 pairs are excluded. Subtraction gives (p-2)^2-(p-2)=(p-2)(p-3).

author: xhigh4
claim: For every prime p>5, the number F(p) in the problem is exactly (p-2)(p-3). Consequently F(p) is congruent to 0 or 2 modulo 5.
evidence: Work in the field of residues modulo p. An infinite sequence is uniquely determined by x=a_1 and y=a_2, since every term is nonzero and the recurrence gives a_{n+2}=(1+a_{n+1})/a_n. Direct substitution gives a_3=(y+1)/x, a_4=(x+y+1)/(xy), and a_5=(x+1)/y; the next two terms are a_6=x and a_7=y. Thus a valid sequence requires and, by periodic repetition of these five displayed terms, is obtained from exactly those pairs x,y for which x,y,x+1,y+1,x+y+1 are all nonzero. Let A be the set of nonzero residues other than -1. There are (p-2)^2 pairs in A^2. Exactly p-2 of them satisfy x+y+1=0: for each x in A, y=-1-x is again in A. Hence F(p)=(p-2)^2-(p-2)=(p-2)(p-3). Since a prime p>5 has residue 1,2,3,or 4 modulo 5, this product is respectively 2,0,0,or 2 modulo 5.

author: high2
claim: For every prime p>5 in the problem, the exact count is F(p)=(p-2)(p-3).
evidence: Work in the field of residues modulo p and write x=a_1, y=a_2. An admissible sequence necessarily has x,y nonzero. The recurrence successively gives a_3=(1+y)/x, so a_3 is nonzero exactly when y is not -1; then a_4=(1+a_3)/y=(1+x+y)/(xy), so a_4 is nonzero exactly when x+y+1 is nonzero; then a_5=(1+a_4)/a_3=(1+x)/y, so a_5 is nonzero exactly when x is not -1. Under these three conditions, a_6=(1+a_5)/a_4=x and a_7=(1+a_6)/a_5=y, so the sequence repeats with period dividing 5 and is admissible forever. Thus admissible sequences are bijective with pairs (x,y) in the nonzero residues satisfying x not equal to -1, y not equal to -1, and x+y+1 not equal to 0. There are (p-2)^2 pairs after the first two exclusions. Among these, x+y+1=0 has exactly p-2 solutions: for each nonzero x not equal to -1, y=-1-x is nonzero and not -1. Subtraction gives F(p)=(p-2)^2-(p-2)=(p-2)(p-3).

author: high3
claim: For every prime p>5, the number of admissible infinite sequences is exactly F(p)=p^2-5p+6.
evidence: Let x=a_1 and y=a_2, viewed modulo p. Since each term is nonzero, the recurrence determines all later terms uniquely. Direct substitution gives a_3=(1+y)/x, a_4=(1+x+y)/(xy), a_5=(1+x)/y, a_6=x, and a_7=y, provided y!=-1, x+y+1!=0, and x!=-1. These three conditions are also necessary because their failure makes respectively a_3, a_4, or a_5 equal to 0, forbidden by the value restriction. Hence admissible sequences are in bijection with pairs (x,y) of nonzero residues outside A={x=-1}, B={y=-1}, C={x+y+1=0}. In the (p-1)^2 nonzero pairs, |A|=|B|=p-1 and |C|=p-2. The only pairwise intersection is A∩B={(-1,-1)}; A∩C and B∩C are empty because they would force y=0 or x=0. Thus |A∪B∪C|=3p-5 and F(p)=(p-1)^2-(3p-5)=p^2-5p+6. author: xhigh2
claim: For every prime p>5 in the problem, the exact count is F(p)=(p-2)(p-3); consequently F(p) is congruent to 0 or 2 modulo 5.
evidence: Identify {1,...,p-1} with the nonzero elements of the finite field F_p. An allowed sequence is uniquely determined by x=a_1 and y=a_2, since a_{n+2}=(1+a_{n+1})/a_n in F_p. Direct substitution gives a_3=(1+y)/x, so validity forces y!=-1; then a_4=(1+a_3)/y=(x+y+1)/(xy), so validity forces x+y+1!=0. Since y+1!=0, a_5=(1+a_4)/a_3=[(x+1)(y+1)/(xy)]/[(y+1)/x]=(x+1)/y, so validity forces x!=-1. Under these three conditions, a_6=(1+a_5)/a_4=[(x+y+1)/y]/[(x+y+1)/(xy)]=x and a_7=(1+a_6)/a_5=(x+1)/[(x+1)/y]=y. Thus the recurrence returns to the initial ordered pair after five steps; determinism shows that the sequence continues forever and is valid. Conversely, every infinite valid sequence necessarily satisfies the three conditions just obtained. Put S=F_p^*\{-1}; it has p-2 elements. Valid sequences therefore correspond bijectively to pairs (x,y) in S^2 with x+y+1!=0. The excluded pairs are exactly (x,-1-x) for x in S, and -1-x belongs to S for every x in S (it is nonzero because x!=-1 and is not -1 because x!=0). Hence there are p-2 excluded pairs, giving F(p)=(p-2)^2-(p-2)=(p-2)(p-3). Since a prime p>5 is congruent to 1,2,3,or 4 modulo 5, this product is respectively congruent to 2,0,0,or 2 modulo 5.

author: xhigh
claim: For an initial pair (x,y) in (F_p^*)^2, an infinite nonzero solution exists if and only if y != -1, x+y+1 != 0, and x != -1; in that case the solution is 5-periodic.
evidence: The recurrence uniquely gives a_3=(1+y)/x. Nonzeroness of a_3 is equivalent to y!=-1. Then a_4=(1+a_3)/y=(x+y+1)/(xy), so nonzeroness of a_4 is equivalent to x+y+1!=0. Under these two conditions, a_5=(1+a_4)/a_3=(x+1)/y, so nonzeroness of a_5 is equivalent to x!=-1. Under all three conditions, a_6=(1+a_5)/a_4=x and a_7=(1+a_6)/a_5=y. Determinism of the recurrence from a consecutive nonzero pair therefore gives a_{n+5}=a_n for every n. Conversely, the five entries x, y, (1+y)/x, (x+y+1)/(xy), (x+1)/y are all nonzero under the three conditions; direct multiplication verifies the recurrence at each of the five cyclic positions, so their periodic repetition is an infinite solution.
